Use “you” and “your” selectively when turning general consequences into an immediate civic or practical question, rather than maintaining a continuously conversational address."},"first-person-plural-family":{"prose":"The plural voice places the argument within a public-interest institution or coalition, while also inviting readers into a shared civic perspective. Use “we” and “our” when stating an organization’s position, describing collective action, or framing access and rights as common concerns."},"contractions":{"prose":"Contractions keep policy criticism accessible and spoken without making it casual; they appear throughout explanatory passages and forceful conclusions. Prefer ordinary contracted forms in the main argumentative flow, particularly when stating what a bill “isn’t,” “won’t,” or “shouldn’t” do."},"uncontracted-negatives":{"prose":"Full negative forms give selected claims extra deliberateness, especially when rejecting a bill’s premise, limiting an apparent safeguard, or distinguishing legal possibility from practical reality. Use uncontracted negatives for consequential pivots and formal rebuttals, while allowing contractions to carry the surrounding conversational cadence."},"first-person-singular-family":{"prose":"Individual self-reference is not a stable organizing stance; the argument ordinarily speaks through an institution, coalition, or public-interest position rather than personal anecdote. Keep the writer’s private viewpoint out of the foreground, reserving singular reference for an occasional narrowly relevant clarification."},"question-marks":{"prose":"Questions function as structured challenges that expose consequences a proposal leaves unanswered, often after the legal or technical setup. Use an occasional question to make an abstract policy risk concrete for readers, then answer or develop it immediately rather than leaving it as theatrical suspense."},"round-parenthetical-spans":{"prose":"Parentheses insert compact qualifications, examples, institutional names, or side information without breaking the main line of reasoning. Place them beside a specific legal or technical claim when the detail improves precision, keeping the sentence’s principal assertion readable outside the aside."},"em-dashes":{"prose":"Em dashes mark sharp pivots, appositives, and compressed qualifications, helping the prose move from a formal claim to its practical consequence. Use them at moments of contrast or emphasis—especially before a consequence or corrective phrase—without turning every sentence into a segmented aside."},"en-dashes":{"prose":"The en dash is not a dependable part of the punctuation system; related ranges and compounds should not be made to carry a special rhetorical function.
